title: Felix and the Inventory
premise: Odile Montrose has tuned the pianos of the Verrecchia house for seven years, learning its secrets through pipes, floorboards, and the silences of the family that pays her to say nothing. When a hidden cache of undelivered letters surfaces behind a wardrobe — letters the late matriarch wrote but never sent — Odile discovers the family's careful architecture of duty was built over an old injustice: a disinherited brother, a forged will, a love the house itself was designed to bury. As she falls for the family's reluctant heir, Tomas, Odile must choose between the survival her silence has bought her and the justice the letters demand. In the end she delivers the letters, the truth fractures the family's inheritance, and she leaves with Tomas — poorer, freer, and finally saying it out loud.
about_author: Vesper Yarrow is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent a decade listening to old houses before turning to fiction. They write about quiet people who keep dangerous knowledge, and live in a drafty building they refuse to insulate.

chapters.title: The Pitch of the House
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She tunes the Verrecchia grand and reads the house through its radiators and settling beams, establishing her uncanny intimacy with the place. The family performs civility around her; she performs invisibility. Emotional beat: the comfort of being needed without being seen.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, flashback-woven. We learn why she keeps her observations to herself: an earlier employer destroyed her reputation when she spoke plainly about what she'd heard. Beat: the price of speech, already paid once.

chapters.title: Tomas Comes Home
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The heir returns for the anniversary of his mother's death, dutiful and hollowed out. He notices Odile properly for the first time — she's the only person in the house who doesn't perform for him. Beat: recognition across a room.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Moving the wardrobe to reach a water-damaged wall, she finds a cavity of unsent letters in the matriarch's hand, addressed to a name no one mentions: Aurelio. She takes one letter — just one. Beat: transgression disguised as accident.

chapters.title: Aurelio
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The letter reveals a brother erased from the family record, cut out by a will signed under circumstances the matriarch herself came to doubt. Odile researches him at the library and finds he died poor, two towns over. Beat: grief for a stranger.

chapters.title: The Second Tuning
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas watches Odile work and catches her hesitating over something; their first real conversation happens over the open piano, all subtext. Beat: attraction sharpened by mutual suspicion of the house.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Counts
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Marthe, the eldest sibling and keeper of the estate's accounts, senses something shifted and begins watching Odile. A chillingly polite exchange establishes Marthe as the house's immune system. Beat: threat wearing gloves.

chapters.title: Letters as Evidence
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She reads more letters at night, learning the matriarch spent her last years trying to undo the forgery and failing against her own family. The youngest sibling, Cato, nearly catches her. Beat: complicity deepening into commitment.

chapters.title: Rain on the Conservatory Roof
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas and Odile shelter from a storm and almost-say-it again, this time together — two people fluent in the same cowardice. He confesses he suspects his inheritance is built on something rotten. Beat: intimacy through shared evasion.

chapters.title: Marthe Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Marthe offers Odile a permanent retainer — generous, binding, conditional on discretion about 'family matters.' It's both bribe and warning. Odile accepts, buying time. Beat: survival priced in silence.

chapters.title: The Forger's Hand
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Comparing the will's signature with the letters' handwriting, Odile confirms the document was coached or coerced — and finds a witness named in the margins: the old gardener, still alive. Beat: the past acquiring a pulse.

chapters.title: The Gardener's Testimony
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile visits the dying gardener, who confirms the matriarch begged him to speak and he chose his pension over the truth. He gives Odile the second copy of the will he kept out of guilt. Beat: another survivor's shame mirroring hers.

chapters.title: Cato's Curiosity
chapters.summary: Cato's POV. The youngest sibling, half-admiring, pieces together that Odile knows something and confronts her not with anger but hunger — he wants out of the family myth too. An uneasy alliance forms. Beat: betrayal becoming contagious.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas tells Odile he loves her in the language of everything except the words; she, holding the will in her bag, realizes telling him means choosing justice over the safety of them both. She says nothing. Beat: love against duty, inverted.

chapters.title: The House Hears Everything
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Marthe discovers the missing letter via a household ledger discrepancy and searches Odile's things while she works. Odile returns to find the room subtly violated — and the remaining letters gone. Beat: dread arriving ahead of consequence.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Marthe's POV. Marthe burns the letters in the study fireplace, keeping only the will's existence deniable, and terminates Odile's contract with impeccable courtesy. But Cato has already photographed three letters. Beat: the machinery of protection grinding forward.

chapters.title: What Odile Knows
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Cato shows Tomas the photographs; Tomas confronts Odile, wounded that she knew and said nothing — repeating the family's oldest sin in miniature. She gives him the gardener's copy of the will. Beat: rupture before repair.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, climax part one. At the family gathering marking the estate transfer, Tomas produces the will and the testimony. Marthe denies, then calculates, then collapses into the truth: their mother wanted it undone and they buried her wish. Beat: the question the whole family arranged itself around, finally asked.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, climax part two. Lawyers say the will is unenforceable after all these years; the remedy must be extralegal — Aurelio's descendants found and provided for, the record corrected by the living, not the courts. Marthe, broken open, agrees to fund it. Beat: justice that law cannot deliver.

chapters.title: Aurelio's People
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She and Tomas trace Aurelio's granddaughter, a schoolteacher living modestly, and make restitution without spectacle. The woman asks Odile why she did it; Odile answers honestly for the first time in the book. Beat: the cost acknowledged, the debt partially paid.

chapters.title: The Last Tuning
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile tunes the piano one final time, the house sounding different now — lighter, less guarded. She and Marthe share a wordless truce; Cato leaves to train as an archivist. Beat: mourning the house even while leaving it.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, coda. On the road out of town, Odile says the thing she has practiced for seven years — plainly, to Tomas, with no furniture between them. The novel ends mid-journey, unresolved in circumstance, resolved in voice. Beat: love chosen over survival, and surviving anyway.
